hypotheses.claim: ORM hydration of each CustomerProfile entity dominates per‑row CPU time.
hypotheses.mechanism: Spring Data JPA maps each row to a CustomerProfile entity, invoking reflection and proxy creation for every column, which costs ~0.2 ms per entity as seen by the linear increase in latency with row count while SQL time stays flat.
evidence: size=1 probe latency 3.7 ms, SQL 0.2 ms, leaving ~3.5 ms per row
size=100 probe latency 21.9 ms, SQL 1.1 ms, leaving ~20.8 ms total (~0.21 ms per row)
rows examined 20000 → 10000 matches, no index used, so DB work minimal
hypotheses.prediction: If the repository method is changed to return projections (interface‑based DTOs) instead of full entities, the per‑row latency will drop by roughly 0.2 ms per row.

hypotheses.claim: Application‑level DTO mapping copies entity fields into response objects per row.
hypotheses.mechanism: CustomerDirectoryService iterates over the list of CustomerProfile entities, creates a CustomerDto for each, copying fields; this loop adds ~0.02 ms per element, evident from the linear latency component beyond ORM.
evidence: Both probes show response body size growing 79 bytes per row, indicating a per‑row object is built
Latency after subtracting ORM cost (~0.2 ms/row) still leaves ~0.02 ms/row, consistent with a lightweight mapping step
hypotheses.prediction: If the service returns the entities directly (skipping DTO creation), the latency for 100 rows will fall by ~2 ms.

hypotheses.claim: JSON serialization of the DTO list adds a per‑row cost.
hypotheses.mechanism: Spring MVC uses Jackson to convert the list of DTOs to JSON; each extra element requires additional buffer allocations and field writes, accounting for ~0.02 ms per row, which together with ORM explains the bulk of the 94 % non‑SQL time.
evidence: Response body size grows ~79 bytes per row, and total latency rises ~0.2 ms per row beyond ORM and mapping
Jackson serialization cost is roughly proportional to output size, matching the observed scaling
hypotheses.prediction: Disabling JSON (e.g., returning plain text) or switching to a faster serializer will reduce the per‑row latency by ~0.02 ms per element.

probes_run.result: Latency 3.7 ms, SQL 0.2 ms, 1 row, 79 B body. Latency scales linearly with rows in the size=100 probe, while SQL time stays flat, indicating per‑row work outside the DB.
Latency 21.9 ms, SQL 1.1 ms, 100 rows, 7712 B body. Linear increase in latency and body size with row count isolates the cost to application layers.
